subject: English
passage: Historians and economists used to believe that medieval European towns during the High Middle Ages (roughly 1000–1300) lacked specialized craft guilds. One reason for this belief was that these scholars misunderstood the economic complexity of medieval urban centers. Guilds typically emerge because different artisans or craftspeople want to trade specialized skills and products they control for skills and products they don't control. Scholars seriously underestimated the economic specialization within medieval towns and thus assumed that ______
prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: guilds likely would not have attracted many members from outside the towns controlled by medieval lords.
choices.B: crafting techniques would have been largely the same throughout medieval towns even if the products people made varied significantly.
choices.C: artisans would join guilds only if they had already mastered their craft and could teach others.
choices.D: guilds would not have enabled medieval craftspeople to acquire many skills or products different from those they already possessed.

explanation:
Choice D is the best answer because it presents the conclusion that most logically follows from the text's discussion of scholars' understanding of medieval economic complexity and craft guilds. The text indicates that scholars used to believe that during the High Middle Ages, medieval European towns didn't have specialized craft guilds. According to the text, scholars held this view because they misunderstood the economic complexity of medieval urban centers. The text points out that people tend to create guilds in order to trade specialized skills and products they don't otherwise control. Craft guilds would have allowed artisans who specialized in one type of work to exchange their expertise for other types of skills and products they didn't possess. The text goes on to say, however, that scholars underestimated the economic specialization within medieval towns, meaning that scholars thought that medieval towns had less diverse crafts and skills than they actually had. Taken together, then, this information suggests that scholars assumed that guilds wouldn't have allowed medieval craftspeople to acquire skills or products different from those they already possessed: that is, if everyone practiced the same crafts, as scholars mistakenly believed, then there wouldn't have been any need for guilds where people could exchange specialized skills and products.

Why B is incorrect:

Choice B is incorrect because the text indicates that scholars underestimated the economic specialization of medieval towns, which suggests that they mistakenly believed that towns had a relatively small array of crafts and skills, not that the products medieval craftspeople made varied significantly throughout the towns. Although the scholars might have assumed that a lack of economic specialization suggests that crafting techniques were largely the same everywhere, the text does not support that they also assumed there was a lot of variation in the products that medieval people made. In fact, the text states that guilds emerge when people want to obtain skills and products they don't already control. If it were the case that scholars assumed that the products medieval craftspeople made varied significantly, this would have led them to conclude that medieval people likely established guilds so they could trade for skills and products they didn't already possess, not that medieval towns lacked specialized craft guilds.
